# Fixture corpus licenses

Generated by `tools/fetch_corpora.py` -- do not hand-edit, re-run the script instead. Every file in `tests/fixtures/*.jsonl` is a ~200-case sample drawn from exactly one source below. Each license was confirmed from a first-party statement (a LICENSE file in the source's own distribution, or a license field in its own dataset card) at fetch time -- see `license_evidence` in the `SOURCES` table of `tools/fetch_corpora.py` for exactly what was checked and where.

Only these licenses may be shipped from this repo: CC BY 4.0, CC BY-SA 4.0. That set -- not the list of source names -- is what the fetch script actually enforces before writing a fixture.

The same metadata is emitted machine-readably as `tests/fixtures/sources.json`, so a benchmark report can print each source's caveat next to its score instead of leaving it here where nobody reading a number will see it.

## LibriSpeech-PC -- `librispeech-pc.jsonl`

- **License:** CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
- **Evidence:** LICENSE.txt inside manifests.tar.gz itself: 'The LibriSpeech-PC Dataset is made available by NVIDIA CORPORATION under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License.'
- **Source:** https://www.openslr.org/145/
- **Revision:** sha256:96d4eae2222b29b66437a21959252419bcd4762e5042e71e023790171054d1c0 (sha256 of manifests.tar.gz)
- **Citation:** A. Meister, M. Novikov, N. Karpov, E. Bakhturina, V. Lavrukhin, B. Ginsburg, "LibriSpeech-PC: Benchmark for Evaluation of Punctuation and Capitalization Capabilities of end-to-end ASR Models," arXiv:2310.02943, 2023.
- **Caveat:** READ speech: LibriVox volunteers reading pre-1928 Gutenberg prose, via the original LibriSpeech corpus. Zero fillers, and a comma distribution drawn from long literary sentences. It measures punctuation/casing restoration and NOTHING about disfluency -- optimizing the formatter against this corpus alone could actively harm real dictation output. Treat it as a regression guard, not a target.
- **Cases:** 200

## Earnings-22 -- `earnings22.jsonl`

- **License:** CC BY-SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
- **Evidence:** earnings22/LICENSE.md in the repo: 'The transcripts and associated text files that are used for alignment in this directory are licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International license.'
- **Source:** https://github.com/revdotcom/speech-datasets/tree/main/earnings22
- **Revision:** c05ab6fd8b4b627d123c922a22a39e993dd37635 (git commit (github.com/revdotcom/speech-datasets))
- **Citation:** M. Del Rio et al., "Earnings-22: A Practical Benchmark for Accents in Speech Recognition," Research in Language 21(3), 2023 (arXiv:2203.15591).
- **Caveat:** Spontaneous speech (earnings calls), real fillers ('um'/'uh' appear as ordinary tokens on BOTH sides here). This entry covers the full 125-call corpus, whose transcripts/nlp_references/*.nlp are verbatim, token-level, punctuation+case-tagged references -- one transcript per call, so on its own it supports kind=punctuation only. The verbatim/non-verbatim PAIR a disfluency fixture needs does exist, for ten of these calls, under earnings22/subset10/ -- see the separate `earnings22-subset10` source, which is where every kind=disfluency case from Earnings-22 comes from. None of the ten subset10 calls appears in the sample here -- asserted in the fetch script -- so the punctuation and disfluency fixtures share no audio and no transcript text.
- **Cases:** 200

## Earnings-22 Subset 10 -- `earnings22-subset10.jsonl`

- **License:** CC BY-SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)
- **Evidence:** earnings22/subset10/LICENSE.md, the subset's OWN license file (not inherited from the parent directory): 'The transcripts and associated text files that are used for alignment in this directory are licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International license.'
- **Source:** https://github.com/revdotcom/speech-datasets/tree/main/earnings22/subset10
- **Revision:** c05ab6fd8b4b627d123c922a22a39e993dd37635 (git commit (github.com/revdotcom/speech-datasets))
- **Citation:** Q. McNamara, M. A. del Rio Fernandez, N. Bhandari, M. Ratajczak, D. Chen, C. Miller, M. Jette, "Style-agnostic evaluation of ASR using multiple reference transcripts," arXiv:2412.07937, 2024 -- the paper describing this subset's creation; the underlying calls are Earnings-22 (Del Rio et al., Research in Language 21(3), 2023).
- **Caveat:** THE VERBATIM/NON-VERBATIM PAIR. Ten Earnings-22 calls were re-transcribed in a second style and shipped under earnings22/subset10/. Its README states the difference first-hand: 'The verbatim transcripts are created by the transcriptionists writing exactly what they hear, including filler words, stutters, interjections (active listening) and repetitions. The nonverbatim transcripts are created by lightly editing for readability without changing the structure or meaning of the speech.' Why it is easy to miss: subset10/verbatim_transcripts/nlp_references/*.nlp are git SYMLINKS (mode 120000) back to ../../../transcripts/nlp_references/*.nlp, so the verbatim half looks identical to the full corpus and only subset10/nonverbatim_transcripts/ is new. Looking only at earnings22/transcripts/ therefore shows one transcript per call and nothing else, which is the wrong conclusion. HOW THE CASES ARE DERIVED, since upstream ships no sentence-level alignment: the two token streams are aligned with difflib, cut into units only where BOTH sides end a sentence at the same aligned token, and a unit is kept only if it is DELETION-ONLY -- the non-verbatim side is the verbatim side with whole tokens deleted and, on each token that survives, punctuation characters deleted; nothing inserted, nothing substituted, nothing re-cased, punctuation included -- AND every deleted run is a recognisable disfluency: a filler ('uh', 'um', ...), an immediate repetition of a word that SURVIVES next to it, or a false start (Rev marks these with a trailing hyphen, e.g. 'curren-'). Punctuation may vanish because that is a mechanical consequence of the deletion -- the commas in 'So, obviously higher margins, uh, excluding those sales.' exist only to set off the filler -- but punctuation that is ADDED ('So' -> 'So,'), SWAPPED ('detail.' -> 'detail?') or used to merge two sentences into one ('CapEx. Um, our guidance' -> 'CapEx, our guidance') is a rewrite and the unit is discarded, as it is where the transcriptionist also reworded ('gonna' -> 'going to'), corrected a mishearing, dropped an ordinary word, or restyled capitalisation. Those are editorial choices a formatter cannot be expected to reproduce, and scoring them would put an unreachable ceiling on the metric. 260 of 4566 candidate units survive (5.7%); the script prints this on every run. WHAT THIS FIXTURE THEREFORE DOES NOT MEASURE, which is a consequence of the filter's construction and not a sampling accident: SELF-CORRECTIONS ('we grew three, sorry, four percent') and RESTARTS that are not hyphen-marked are absent by design. A correction replaces one word with a different one, so the aligner sees a `replace` and the unit is discarded; an abandoned phrase that Rev did not mark with a trailing hyphen is an unexplained deletion and is discarded too. The tag counts on the committed sample show the shape of what is left: filler 152, repetition 79, false-start 13 out of 200 cases. So this fixture measures REMOVAL OF FILLERS AND REPETITIONS well, false starts thinly, and self-corrections not at all -- and it does not measure the full verbatim-to-readable rewrite Rev's transcriptionists actually performed. Disfl-QA is the complement here: over 90% of ITS disfluencies are corrections and restarts, but it is written text rather than speech.
- **Cases:** 200

## Disfl-QA -- `disflqa.jsonl`

- **License:** CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
- **Evidence:** README.md, '## License' section: 'Disfl-QA dataset is licensed under CC BY 4.0.'
- **Source:** https://github.com/google-research-datasets/Disfl-QA
- **Revision:** 1f0c16171c77b3d3408be92c485f11b8998a9189 (git commit (github.com/google-research-datasets/Disfl-QA))
- **Citation:** A. Gupta, J. Xu, S. Upadhyay, D. Yang, M. Faruqui, "Disfl-QA: A Benchmark Dataset for Understanding Disfluencies in Question Answering," Findings of ACL, 2021.
- **Caveat:** ~12k (disfluent, original) question pairs built on SQuAD-v2; over 90% of disfluencies are corrections or restarts. Written text, not ASR transcripts -- both sides start already cased and punctuated, so `verbatim` here carries the disfluent question in its original casing/punctuation and `input` is `tools/fetch_corpora.py`'s lowercase/unpunctuated simulation of it.
- **Cases:** 200

## Indic DiarBench (sarvamai/indic-diarbench) -- `indic-diarbench.jsonl`

- **License:** CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
- **Evidence:** Hugging Face dataset card metadata, machine-readable: cardData.license == "cc-by-4.0" (confirmed via https://huggingface.co/api/datasets/sarvamai/indic-diarbench).
- **Source:** https://huggingface.co/datasets/sarvamai/indic-diarbench
- **Revision:** 92877bad8aab6e598167d91c6ee02aa8ca6ede09 (Hugging Face repo SHA (huggingface.co/datasets/sarvamai/indic-diarbench))
- **Citation:** Sarvam AI, "Indic DiarBench: A Multilingual Joint Diarization and ASR Benchmark for Indian Languages," Interspeech 2026 (arXiv:2607.23808).
- **Caveat:** REGIONAL-LANGUAGE REGRESSION GUARD, NOT A QUALITY TARGET -- this project's stated priority is English formatting first. Natural multi-speaker conversational Hindi with real Devanagari danda punctuation, published by this app's own ASR vendor. Scoped to the Hindi config only, out of the 22 languages the full benchmark covers, and audio is never downloaded, only the `annotated_transcript` text. Segments that are pure non-speech tags (<noise>, <unintelligible>, <background_speech>) are dropped rather than treated as text. MEASURED ANNOTATION ARTIFACT, do not read a score here without it: this benchmark glosses code-mixed and spelled-out words by appending the Latin-script or numeric form in parentheses -- 'एग्जेग्टली(exactly)', 'तीस(30)'. Counted over the committed sample, 69.5% of cases contain at least one such gloss and parentheses are 956 of the 1432 restorable punctuation marks (67%) -- so a majority of the punctuation 'restoration' being scored is really reinstating a transcription convention, not a formatting behaviour any dictation user wants (no formatter can derive '(30)' from the spelled-out word). Those cases are TAGGED rather than dropped, because dropping them would shrink an intentional regression guard: `english-gloss` marks a case containing any such gloss, and `gloss-dominated` marks the subset where parentheses are at least half that case's punctuation. A report should separate them, and should not present the gloss-dominated subset as a formatting-quality number.
- **Cases:** 200

## Researched but NOT included

### DISCO (vineet2104/DISCO)

- **Source:** https://github.com/vineet2104/DISCO
- **Claimed license:** CC BY 4.0 (as declared on the paper, arXiv:2310.16749)
- **Why excluded:** No first-party license grant could be found for the DATA. Re-verified against the repository's full recursive git tree at commit b91a9e8d43cbfbefb9d7b0ff836c18d9a676943d (17 entries, untruncated): no LICENSE/COPYING file anywhere, and no license section in README.md. WHAT THE CC BY 4.0 ON THE PAPER ACTUALLY IS: arXiv:2310.16749 really does declare CC BY 4.0 on its abs page, and that is an author-selected license, not a default -- arXiv states that permission 'is granted through a license, chosen by the submitter', from CC BY 4.0 / CC BY-SA 4.0 / CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 / CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 / arXiv's own perpetual non-exclusive license 1.0 / CC Zero, per version (verified against https://arxiv.org/help/license). It is a deliberate grant and it covers THE ARTICLE. It says nothing about a dataset distributed from a separate GitHub repository, which is what would actually be redistributed here, and that repository carries no grant at all. Reading a license on the paper as a license on the data is exactly the mistake this allow-list exists to prevent. Do not move this into SOURCES without an explicit, first-party license statement covering the data -- e.g. the authors adding a LICENSE file, or a written grant. If that ever happens: the data is data/labeled-data/{English,Hindi}.xlsx, sheet '{en,hi}-disfluent-sentences-labelled', columns 'Disfluent Sentence' -> input source and 'Fluent Sentence' / 'Hindi Fluent Sentence' -> target (needs openpyxl to read; verified present but not vendored here since this path is unused).

## Never use (verified CC BY-NC / LDC-paid / punctuation-stripped -- do not add)

- **fisher** -- LDC paid license, not redistributable.
- **indicvoices** -- Empirically punctuation-stripped.
- **indicvoices-r** -- Empirically punctuation-stripped.
- **iwslt** -- Constituent sets are CC BY-NC-ND -- non-commercial.
- **kathbath** -- Empirically punctuation-stripped.
- **must-c** -- CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 -- non-commercial, no derivatives.
- **nptel2020** -- AI4Bharat's NPTEL2020: empirically punctuation-stripped AND all-caps.
- **shrutilipi** -- Empirically punctuation-stripped.
- **sponspeech** -- CC BY-NC 4.0 -- non-commercial.
- **svarah** -- No stated license anywhere, AND empirically punctuation-stripped -- would not measure formatting restoration even if licensing were resolved.
- **switchboard** -- LDC paid license, not redistributable.
- **ted-lium** -- CC BY-NC-ND 3.0 -- non-commercial, no derivatives.
